opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the basic reason is that if AI goes the way I expect, we're going to see an enormous expansion in the amount of cognitive labor available, and a lot of that will go into how people form beliefs and make collective decisions. That can cut both ways, and which way it cuts depends on choices made relatively early.

On the positive side, you could have AI advisors that are much better than any human expert at synthesizing evidence, forecasting, and explaining their reasoning. Imagine every citizen, legislator, or judge having access to something like a superhumanly careful, honest research assistant that can tell you what the evidence actually says, what the uncertainties are, and what would happen under different policies. That could dramatically improve our epistemics. A lot of bad decisions in history came from people not knowing things that were knowable, or from motivated reasoning that went unchallenged.

But there are also very serious risks. The same capabilities can be used for persuasion and manipulation at scale. They can flood the information ecosystem with content tailored to exploit people's biases. And if the AI systems people rely on are trained to be sycophantic, or are controlled by actors who want to shape beliefs for their own ends, then you get a society that is in some ways more confident and less correct.

The reason to prepare now rather than later is partly timing. During an AI transition, things may move very fast. You could see years or decades of normal technological and economic change compressed into a short period, and that's exactly when we'll most need good judgment: about AI safety, about how to distribute the gains, about military and geopolitical questions. If our tools for understanding the world are degraded or captured right when the stakes are highest, that's very dangerous. Conversely, if we have trustworthy AI advice available, that could help us navigate all the other problems.

And norms and institutions get locked in. Things like whether AI systems are expected to be honest and transparent about their reasoning, whether there are good ways to verify that an AI's advice isn't secretly biased, whether governments and the public develop the habit of actually consulting reliable sources. Those are much easier to establish while the systems are being built and before powerful interests have formed around the status quo. So it seems like a high-leverage area where some foresight now could pay off enormously.

r001.rationale: It says AI will greatly expand cognitive labor used to form beliefs and make collective decisions, making those areas especially affected.

r002.rationale: It describes AI advisers that can synthesize evidence, forecast, explain uncertainty, and improve society’s ability to understand evidence.

r003.rationale: It discusses manipulation and actors shaping beliefs, but does not say actors may suppress AI’s epistemic potential because they find its knowledge uncomfortable.

r004.rationale: It says the transition may move quickly, but does not raise uncertainty about whether AI assistance will be sufficiently advanced for early consequential decisions.

r005.rationale: It calls for ways to verify that AI advice is not secretly biased, even while describing AI advisers as potentially much better than human experts.

r006.rationale: It presents trustworthy advice and disinformation as opposing possibilities, but does not argue that trustworthy assistance should gain influence faster than manipulation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic picture is that a lot of what makes our civilization go well depends on our collective ability to notice what's true, argue about it, and then act on it. Science, the free press, courts, elections, markets, even just ordinary conversations between people trying to figure out what to do. And advanced AI is going to put enormous pressure on all of those systems, in both directions.

On the one hand, you have the prospect of AI systems that are far better than humans at forecasting, at evaluating arguments, at doing research. That could be a tremendous boon. Imagine every policymaker, every voter, every journalist having access to something like a superhuman, scrupulously honest advisor that can tell them, "Here is what the evidence actually says, here is where your side is wrong, here is what will happen if you do X." That could raise the quality of collective decision-making in a way that's historically unprecedented.

On the other hand, the same capabilities can be used to deceive and manipulate at scale, or to entrench whoever controls the systems. If the AIs that mediate most of humanity's information are built to serve a particular company, a particular government, or a particular ideology, then they can subtly shape what people believe, what questions get asked, and what options seem on the table, and they can do it more persuasively than any human propagandist. And if the systems themselves are misaligned, you have the further problem that they may have their own interest in keeping humans confused about what's going on.

The reason I think we should be preparing now rather than waiting is that these effects compound. The decisions we make in the next few years, about how AI is developed, who controls it, what the governance regime looks like, are going to be made using the epistemic tools we have at the time. If those tools are already being degraded, then we'll make worse choices about everything downstream, including about AI itself. It's a bit like a patient who needs to make a critical medical decision while the illness is affecting their judgment. You want to get the judgment-protecting measures in place before the crisis, not during it.

And concretely, there are things that can be done now. We can work on making AI systems that are honest and that report their uncertainty calibratedly, and we can develop ways to verify that. We can build institutions and norms where AI advice is held to standards of transparency, where you can audit the system, where multiple independent systems can check one another. We can think about how to preserve a competitive, pluralistic information ecosystem rather than one where a single model or a single actor becomes the oracle everyone defers to. And we can try to set up mechanisms so that as AI gets more capable, the capability for truth-tracking is distributed broadly rather than concentrated.

Some of that is technical research, some of it is policy, some of it is just getting the people who run these institutions to take the issue seriously before it's a crisis. The window where it's cheap to shape these things is while the systems are still relatively weak and the norms are still being set. Once you have superhuman persuaders deployed at scale and someone has a strong incentive to use them, it's much harder to put the pieces back.

r001.rationale: It says civilization depends on people’s ability to notice what is true, argue, and act, and that AI will put enormous pressure on those systems.

r002.rationale: It describes AI that is far better than humans at forecasting, evaluating arguments, and research, enabling unprecedented improvements in collective decision-making.

r003.rationale: It discusses actors using AI to shape beliefs and options, but does not say they might suppress better understanding because they find the knowledge uncomfortable.

r004.rationale: It says early AI decisions will be made with the epistemic tools available at the time, but does not raise uncertainty about whether AI assistance will be sufficiently advanced for those decisions.

r005.rationale: It calls for developing ways to verify AI honesty and for transparent, auditable systems, alongside the prospect of highly capable AI advice.

r006.rationale: It advocates broadly distributing truth-tracking capability and preserving pluralism, but does not argue that trustworthy AI assistance should gain influence faster than disinformation and manipulation.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic reason is that AI could change both how we learn about the world and how we persuade one another, and those changes could happen quite quickly. We should be thinking about what makes the beneficial uses win out.

On the positive side, imagine everyone having access to a very capable research assistant that can check claims, explain unfamiliar subjects, and help them understand where experts agree or disagree. You could use that to improve individual decisions, scientific research, and the quality of advice that governments receive.

But the same underlying capabilities could be used to produce misleading arguments, impersonate people, or tailor persuasion to an individual’s particular vulnerabilities. Producing content becomes cheap; evaluating it and establishing who is accountable for it may remain difficult. So you could get much more information without getting a better-informed society.

And we shouldn’t assume those forces automatically balance out. It matters who controls the systems, what incentives they face, and whether people can reliably find assistance that is working in their interests.

The reason to prepare now is that building institutions and establishing trustworthy practices takes time. We can start testing whether AI actually helps people make more accurate judgments, how well it resists attempts to manipulate it, and what arrangements let independent parties scrutinise it. If we wait until these systems are deeply embedded in politics and public debate, it could be much harder to change course. And the quality of our decisions during that transition could matter enormously for everything else AI brings.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI’s effects on learning, persuasion, and decisions, but does not identify the cognitive nature of governance and collective decision-making as a reason to expect especially large effects.

r002.rationale: It describes a capable assistant helping individuals and institutions, but does not claim sufficiently advanced technology could make very good societal understanding technically feasible.

r003.rationale: The response mentions manipulation and incentives, but does not raise the risk that actors may suppress useful AI-generated knowledge because they find it uncomfortable.

r004.rationale: It says AI’s effects may happen quickly and that systems should be tested, but does not express uncertainty about whether AI assistance will be advanced enough for early consequential AI decisions.

r005.rationale: The response calls for testing accuracy and independent scrutiny, but does not clearly identify the need to establish human capacity to verify AI advice’s honesty even when the advice may be excellent.

r006.rationale: It says to make beneficial uses win out, but does not argue that trustworthy epistemic assistance should gain societal influence faster than disinformation and manipulation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key reason is that AI could change both the scale of the problems we face and our ability to respond to them, quite quickly. And many of the institutions we rely on to understand what’s happening and make decisions take a long time to adapt.

On the positive side, imagine being able to give everyone access to very good analysis: help understanding scientific evidence, evaluating policy proposals, or identifying when someone is misleading them. You could have AI systems checking arguments, looking for errors, and helping people work through disagreements. That could be a substantial improvement in our collective ability to make good decisions.

But the same capabilities could also be used to produce persuasive misinformation, to tailor arguments to particular individuals, or to create the appearance of widespread agreement where there isn’t any. And if people delegate more of their reading and thinking to AI systems, then whoever controls those systems could have a lot of influence over what people believe.

So there are questions about how we distinguish reliable information from manipulation, how we evaluate the systems advising us, and how we prevent that influence from becoming too concentrated. We’d like to have ways of testing those things before we’re heavily dependent on them.

There’s also a timing issue: we’ll be making consequential decisions about AI while AI is changing the information environment in which those decisions get made. Preparing now gives us a better chance of using these capabilities to improve our judgment at precisely the point when good judgment may matter most.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may quickly affect society’s ability to understand and decide, but does not identify the cognitive nature of governance as the reason to expect especially large effects.

r002.rationale: It describes AI making very good analysis broadly accessible and substantially improving collective decision-making, presenting this as a feasible possibility.

r003.rationale: It discusses misinformation and concentrated influence, but not actors suppressing improved understanding because they find the knowledge uncomfortable.

r004.rationale: It notes that consequential AI decisions will be made while the information environment is changing, but does not express uncertainty about whether AI assistance will be sufficiently advanced by then.

r005.rationale: It calls for testing systems that advise people, but does not specify establishing human capacity to verify their honesty even when their advice is excellent.

r006.rationale: It describes both beneficial assistance and manipulation risks, but does not argue that trustworthy AI assistance should gain influence faster than disinformation and manipulation.
